shchi.name: Shchi
shchi.summary: A Russian cabbage soup, made sour with sauerkraut or green with sorrel and similar plants, and historically a staple food eaten across all social classes.

polish-lithuanian-commonwealth.name: Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth
polish-lithuanian-commonwealth.summary: A federative union of the Kingdom of Poland and Grand Duchy of Lithuania from 1569 to 1795, one of Europe's largest and most populous states, known for its elective monarchy called the Golden Liberty.

galicia-eastern-europe.name: Galicia
galicia-eastern-europe.summary: A historical region spanning southeastern Poland and western Ukraine, named after the medieval city of Halych, once part of the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth and later Austria's Kingdom of Galicia and Lodomeria.

izba.name: Izba
izba.summary: A traditional Russian countryside dwelling, often a log house, built close to the road within a farmstead yard that also held a garden and barn.

kasha.name: Kasha
kasha.summary: A porridge usually made from buckwheat, called kasha in Slavic languages, where it can also mean any cooked grain and was long a Russian household staple.

cathedral-of-the-nativity-of-the-theotok.name: Cathedral of the Nativity of the Theotokos
cathedral-of-the-nativity-of-the-theotok.summary: A World Heritage cathedral in Suzdal, Russia, built under Vladimir II Monomakh in the late 11th century, among the finest examples of Russian medieval architecture.
cathedral-of-the-nativity-of-the-theotok.source_title: Cathedral of the Nativity of the Theotokos, Suzdal

white-monuments-of-vladimir-and-suzdal.name: White Monuments of Vladimir and Suzdal
white-monuments-of-vladimir-and-suzdal.summary: A UNESCO World Heritage Site of eight medieval limestone churches, a monastery, a castle, and a gate built in Vladimir Oblast, Russia in the late 12th and early 13th centuries.
white-monuments-of-vladimir-and-suzdal.source_title: White Monuments of Vladimir and Suzdal

suzdal.name: Suzdal
suzdal.summary: A town in Vladimir Oblast, Russia, that became capital of the Rostov-Suzdal principality in the early 12th century, a forerunner of the Russian state; now part of Russia's historic Golden Ring.

novgorod-republic.name: Novgorod Republic
novgorod-republic.summary: A city-state in northwestern Russia from the 12th to 15th centuries, governed by an elected assembly rather than a strong prince, and long a center of Russian art and culture.

vladimir-suzdal.name: Vladimir-Suzdal
vladimir-suzdal.summary: Russian principality (originally called Suzdal, later Vladimir) that emerged from the breakup of Kievan Rus' and became the leading northeastern Rus' power before fragmenting by the late 13th century.

pskov.name: Pskov
pskov.summary: One of Russia's oldest cities, on the Velikaya River near the Estonian border; it was capital of the medieval Pskov Republic and a Hanseatic trading post before joining the Grand Duchy of Moscow.

yuriev-monastery.name: Yuriev Monastery
yuriev-monastery.summary: Usually cited as Russia's oldest monastery, standing near Novgorod on the Volkhov River; once the most important monastery in the medieval Novgorod Republic.

vsevolod-i-of-kiev.name: Vsevolod I of Kiev
vsevolod-i-of-kiev.summary: Grand Prince of Kiev from 1078 until his death in 1093.

mstislav-i-of-kiev.name: Mstislav the Great
mstislav-i-of-kiev.summary: Grand Prince of Kiev from 1125 until his death in 1132, after which the Kievan state began quickly breaking apart into rival principalities.

vladimir-ii-monomakh.name: Vladimir II Monomakh
vladimir-ii-monomakh.summary: Grand Prince of Kiev from 1113 to 1125 who led 83 campaigns against the Cuman Polovtsians and is venerated as a saint in the Eastern Orthodox Church; distinct from Saint Vladimir the Great.

yuri-ii-of-vladimir.name: Yuri II of Vladimir
yuri-ii-of-vladimir.summary: Fourth Grand Prince of Vladimir (r. 1212–1216, 1218–1238) who ruled Vladimir-Suzdal during the Mongol invasion of Kievan Rus' and founded Nizhny Novgorod.

golden-gate-vladimir.name: Golden Gate, Vladimir
golden-gate-vladimir.summary: City gate in Vladimir, Russia, built 1158–1164, the only substantially preserved ancient Russian city gate and now a UNESCO World Heritage site.

ivan-iii-of-russia.name: Ivan III
ivan-iii-of-russia.summary: Grand Prince of Moscow from 1462 to 1505, known as Ivan the Great, who expanded Russian territory, ended Tatar dominance in 1480, and laid the foundations of the centralized Russian state.

p-ock.name: Płock
p-ock.summary: A city in central Poland on the Vistula river that was the capital of Poland from 1079 to 1138 and later the main center of medieval Mazovia.

euthymius-ii-of-novgorod.name: Euthymius II of Novgorod
euthymius-ii-of-novgorod.summary: Archbishop of Novgorod from 1429 to 1458, remembered as one of the city's most prolific patrons of art and architecture.

knyaz.name: Knyaz
knyaz.summary: A historical Slavic noble and royal title, usually translated as prince, king or duke depending on context, derived from the Germanic word for king.

yuri-dolgorukiy.name: Yuri Dolgorukiy
yuri-dolgorukiy.summary: 12th-century prince of Rostov and Suzdal (c. 1099–1157) whose building programme turned the principality into the power that became Muscovy; twice briefly ruled as Grand Prince of Kiev.

shuysky.name: Shuisky family
shuysky.summary: Russian family of boyars and tsars, a branch of the Rurikids, whose member Vasili Shuisky ruled as tsar from 1606 to 1610 during the Time of Troubles.

cathedral-of-saint-sophia-novgorod.name: Cathedral of St Sophia
cathedral-of-saint-sophia-novgorod.summary: The cathedral church of the Metropolitan of Novgorod in Russia, the mother church of the Novgorodian Eparchy.

antoniev-monastery.name: Antoniev Monastery
antoniev-monastery.summary: A major medieval monastery in Novgorod, Russia, whose Church of the Nativity of the Mother of God was built between 1117 and 1119 and is one of the few 12th-century buildings surviving in Russia.

novgorod-detinets.name: Novgorod Kremlin
novgorod-detinets.summary: A fortified complex on the Volkhov River in Veliky Novgorod, Russia, also known as the Novgorod Detinets.

yaroslav-s-court.name: Yaroslav's Court
yaroslav-s-court.summary: A princely compound in Veliky Novgorod, Russia, now the area around the Trade Side, including St. Nicholas Cathedral and two other churches.

andrey-bogolyubsky.name: Andrey Bogolyubsky
andrey-bogolyubsky.summary: Andrey Bogolyubsky: Prince of Vladimir-Suzdal from 1157 until his death in 1174, who took part in the capture of Kiev in 1149, and whose son later led the sack of Kiev in 1169; canonized in 1702.

ivan-the-great-bell-tower.name: Ivan the Great Bell Tower
ivan-the-great-bell-tower.summary: An 81-metre church tower in the Moscow Kremlin, its tallest structure, built in 1508 to serve three cathedrals that had no belfries of their own.

palace-of-facets.name: Palace of Facets
palace-of-facets.summary: The oldest preserved secular building in Moscow, on Cathedral Square in the Kremlin, once the main banquet reception hall of the Russian tsars.

dmitry-donskoy.name: Dmitry Donskoy
dmitry-donskoy.summary: Prince of Moscow from 1359 and Grand Prince of Vladimir from 1362 to 1389, the first Moscow prince to openly defy Mongol rule; his nickname 'Donskoy' honors his 1380 victory at the Don River.

mamai.name: Mamai
mamai.summary: Turco-Mongol military commander and kingmaker who dominated the Golden Horde in the 1360s and 1370s without ever becoming khan himself. His defeat at the Battle of Kulikovo in 1380 marked the start of the Horde's decline and his own downfall.

golden-horde.name: Golden Horde
golden-horde.summary: Mongol, later Turkicized khanate (also called the Ulus of Jochi) that split from the Mongol Empire in the 13th century and ruled from Siberia to Eastern Europe until fragmenting after 1396.

kulikovo-field.name: Kulikovo Field
kulikovo-field.summary: Field in Russia's Tula Oblast where the Battle of Kulikovo was fought in 1380, a decisive Russian victory over the Golden Horde.

jebe.name: Jebe
jebe.summary: A prominent Mongol general under Genghis Khan (died c. 1224), originally an enemy soldier who became one of his greatest commanders and helped expand the Mongol Empire.

subutai.name: Subutai
subutai.summary: Mongol general (c. 1175–1248) and chief military strategist for Genghis Khan and Ögedei Khan, who directed over 20 campaigns and conquered more territory than any other commander in history.

kalchyk-river.name: Kalka River
kalchyk-river.summary: A river in present-day Ukraine, historically known as the Kalka, site of the 1223 battle in which Mongol forces defeated a coalition of Rus' princes.

mstislav-mstislavich.name: Mstislav the Bold
mstislav-mstislavich.summary: A prince of Tmutarakan and Chernigov, one of the Rus' princes of Kievan Rus' in the decades before the Mongol invasions, who died around 1228.

mstislav-iii-of-kiev.name: Mstislav III of Kiev
mstislav-iii-of-kiev.summary: A prince who held several Rus' cities before becoming Grand Prince of Kiev from 1212 until his death in 1223.

alexander-nevsky.name: Alexander Nevsky
alexander-nevsky.summary: Prince of Novgorod and Grand Prince of Vladimir (1221–1263), famed for defeating Swedish and German invaders and later canonized as a Russian Orthodox saint.

battle-of-the-neva.name: Battle of the Neva
battle-of-the-neva.summary: A battle on 15 July 1240 in which Novgorod and Karelian forces repelled an invading Swedish force on the Neva River, known chiefly from Russian sources.

battle-on-the-ice.name: Battle on the Ice
battle-on-the-ice.summary: A battle fought on the frozen Lake Peipus on 5 April 1242, in which Prince Alexander Nevsky's Novgorod and Vladimir forces defeated the Livonian Order, later seen as pivotal between Catholic and Orthodox power.

kievan-rus.name: Kievan Rus'
kievan-rus.summary: The first East Slavic state, later a group of principalities, spanning the late 9th to mid-13th century from the White Sea to the Black Sea under the Rurik dynasty.

cumans.name: Cumans
cumans.summary: A Turkic nomadic people from Central Asia who dominated the steppe north of the Black Sea, becoming powerful warriors who influenced medieval Rus', Hungary and the Balkans.

mikhail-ii-of-tver.name: Mikhail of Tver
mikhail-ii-of-tver.summary: Grand Prince of Tver (1368–1399) who briefly held the title Grand Prince of Vladimir and, backed by his brother-in-law the Grand Duke of Lithuania, was among the last princes to seriously challenge Moscow for that title.

jarlig.name: Jarlig
jarlig.summary: A written edict or license issued by Mongol and Chinggisid rulers, used from the mid-13th to mid-15th centuries to authorize princes of Rus to rule.

tver.name: Tver
tver.summary: A Russian city on the Volga River northwest of Moscow, once capital of a powerful medieval state, known as Kalinin from 1931 to 1990.

nizhny-novgorod.name: Nizhny Novgorod
nizhny-novgorod.summary: A Russian city founded in 1221 at the meeting of the Oka and Volga rivers, a major trade centre from 1817 and later, as Gorky, an important Soviet industrial city.

ryazan.name: Ryazan
ryazan.summary: A city on the Oka River in central Russia, southeast of Moscow, that grew from the medieval capital of the Principality of Ryazan, razed by the Mongols in 1237.

bolghar.name: Bolghar
bolghar.summary: Intermittent capital of Volga Bulgaria from the 10th to 13th centuries on the Volga River; its ruins are now a UNESCO World Heritage site.

haji-i-giray.name: Haci I Giray
haji-i-giray.summary: Founder of the Crimean Khanate and the Giray dynasty, ruling from about 1441 until his death in 1466 while fighting off rival warlords as the Golden Horde broke apart.

crimean-khanate.name: Crimean Khanate
crimean-khanate.summary: A Crimean Tatar state founded by Hacı I Giray in 1441 that at its height stretched from Bessarabia to the North Caucasus, before being annexed by Russia in 1783.

chinggisids.name: Chinggisids
chinggisids.summary: The descendants of Genghis Khan and his wife Börte, who by tradition were considered the only legitimate rulers of the Mongol Empire and its successor states, a rule that lasted until 1847.

primary-chronicle.name: Primary Chronicle
primary-chronicle.summary: A chronicle of Kievan Rus' history from about 850 to 1110, compiled around the 1110s and considered a fundamental source for the earliest history of the East Slavs.

nestor-the-chronicler.name: Nestor the Chronicler
nestor-the-chronicler.summary: A monk at the Monastery of the Caves in Kiev (c. 1056–1114) credited with two hagiographies, though modern scholars doubt his long-attributed authorship of the Primary Chronicle.

church-slavonic.name: Church Slavonic
church-slavonic.summary: A South Slavic liturgical language descended from 9th- to 10th-century Old Church Slavonic, still used today in Eastern Orthodox worship across many Slavic countries.

bylina.name: Bylina
bylina.summary: A traditional Russian oral epic poem loosely based on history but embellished with fantasy, originating in the era of Kievan Rus'.

ostromir-gospels.name: Ostromir Gospels
ostromir-gospels.summary: The oldest dated book from Kievan Rus', created in 1056 or 1057 by the deacon Gregory for his patron Ostromir, likely as a gift for a monastery.

ostromir.name: Ostromir
ostromir.summary: Posadnik (governor) of Novgorod from 1054 to 1057, who commissioned the Ostromir Gospels, the oldest precisely dated Russian manuscript.

posadnik.name: Posadnik
posadnik.summary: The highest official in the medieval Russian cities of Novgorod and Pskov, originally a prince's representative who became an elected burgomaster.

veliky-novgorod.name: Veliky Novgorod
veliky-novgorod.summary: One of Russia's oldest cities, first mentioned in the 9th century; center of the Novgorod Republic from 1136 to 1478 and a major trading link to northwestern Europe via the Hanseatic League.

novgorod-codex.name: Novgorod Codex
novgorod-codex.summary: The oldest known book of the Kievan Rus', a wax-tablet palimpsest found in Novgorod in 2000 and dated to around 1000 CE, reused repeatedly by its owner over two or three decades.

hilarion-of-kiev.name: Hilarion of Kiev
hilarion-of-kiev.summary: The first non-Greek Metropolitan of Kiev and all Rus', holding the post around the time of the 11th-century split between the Eastern and Western churches.

sermon-on-law-and-grace.name: Sermon on Law and Grace
sermon-on-law-and-grace.summary: A sermon written by Hilarion, metropolitan of Kiev, around 1037 to 1050, one of the earliest Slavonic texts and highly influential on later literature in Kievan Rus'.

great-khan.name: Khagan
great-khan.summary: A title of imperial rank in Mongolic and Turkic languages, equal in status to emperor, used for rulers of a khaganate such as the Mongol Empire and its successor Yuan dynasty.

vladimir-the-great.name: Vladimir the Great
vladimir-the-great.summary: Prince of Novgorod from 970 and Grand Prince of Kiev from 978 until 1015, who converted to Christianity in 988 and Christianized Kievan Rus'; canonised as a saint by both the Catholic and Orthodox churches.

yaroslav-the-wise.name: Yaroslav the Wise
yaroslav-the-wise.summary: Grand Prince of Kiev from 1019 to 1054, who allied with Scandinavian states, built Saint Sophia Cathedral, and patronized early Old East Slavic literature.

kyiv-pechersk-lavra.name: Kyiv Pechersk Lavra
kyiv-pechersk-lavra.summary: A historic Eastern Christian monastery founded as a cave monastery in Kyiv in the 11th century, long a leading religious center in Eastern Europe and an early printing hub in Ukraine.

boris-and-gleb.name: Boris and Gleb
boris-and-gleb.summary: The first saints canonized in Kievan Rus' after its Christianization.

theodosius-of-kiev.name: Theodosius of Kiev
theodosius-of-kiev.summary: 11th-century saint who brought communal monastic life to Kievan Rus' and, with Anthony of Kiev, founded the Kiev Caves Monastery.

the-tale-of-igor-s-campaign.name: The Tale of Igor's Campaign
the-tale-of-igor-s-campaign.summary: An anonymous Old East Slavic epic poem, likely from the late 12th century, describing a failed raid by Prince Igor Svyatoslavich against the Polovtsians; it later inspired Alexander Borodin's opera Prince Igor (1890).

life-of-alexander-nevsky.name: Life of Alexander Nevsky
life-of-alexander-nevsky.summary: An Old East Slavic hagiography about Alexander Nevsky, composed in stages from the late 13th to mid-15th century, blending political realism with hagiographic ideals.

daniel-the-traveller.name: Daniel the Traveller
daniel-the-traveller.summary: The first travel writer from Kievan Rus, known for journeying to the Holy Land after the First Crusade and leaving an important account of the region.

the-tale-of-the-destruction-of-ryazan.name: The Tale of the Destruction of Ryazan
the-tale-of-the-destruction-of-ryazan.summary: A Russian literary work, compiled from earlier manuscripts, describing the Mongols' capture of the city of Ryazan under Batu in 1237.
the-tale-of-the-destruction-of-ryazan.source_title: The Tale of the Destruction of Ryazan

charles-j-halperin.name: Charles J. Halperin
charles-j-halperin.summary: American historian, born 1946, specializing in the medieval history of Eastern Europe, particularly the Golden Horde, Kievan Rus' and early Muscovy.

peter-benjamin-golden.name: Peter B. Golden
peter-benjamin-golden.summary: American historian and professor emeritus at Rutgers University, specializing in Turkic, Central Asian and Mongol history.

khazars.name: Khazars
khazars.summary: A semi-nomadic Turkic people who built a major trading empire from about 650 to 965 CE spanning southern Russia, Ukraine, and Kazakhstan, with a ruling elite that converted to Judaism in the 8th century.

birch-bark-manuscript.name: Birch bark manuscripts
birch-bark-manuscript.summary: Documents written on the outer layer of birch bark, used before mass-produced paper, with examples ranging from 1st-century Buddhist texts to 11th–15th century Russian letters found in Novgorod.

old-east-slavic.name: Old East Slavic
old-east-slavic.summary: A language used by the East Slavs from the 7th–8th to 13th–14th centuries that later split into the Russian, Ukrainian and Belarusian/Ruthenian languages.

russell-zguta.name: Russell Zguta
russell-zguta.summary: American historian, born in 1949, and professor emeritus at the University of Missouri.

skomorokh.name: Skomorokh
skomorokh.summary: A medieval East Slavic performer who sang, danced, played music and acted, later pushed out of Kiev by clergy after Christianization.

vladimir-russia.name: Vladimir, Russia
vladimir-russia.summary: City on the Klyazma River in Russia, about 200 km east of Moscow, with a population of roughly 350,000.

sit-river.name: Sit River
sit-river.summary: A 159-kilometre river in Russia flowing through Tver and Yaroslavl oblasts into the Rybinsk Reservoir, formerly a tributary of the Mologa.

hanseatic-league.name: Hanseatic League
hanseatic-league.summary: A medieval network of merchant guilds and trading towns across Central and Northern Europe, growing from Lübeck in the 12th century to nearly 200 settlements that came to dominate Baltic and North Sea trade.

great-horde.name: Great Horde
great-horde.summary: The rump state of the Golden Horde, centered at Sarai on the lower Volga from the mid-15th century to 1502, whose forces' retreat before Ivan III marked the end of Tatar rule over Russia.

ivan-the-terrible.name: Ivan IV
ivan-the-terrible.summary: Grand Prince of Moscow from 1533 and Russia's first Tsar from 1547 until his death in 1584, known as Ivan the Terrible; his reign turned Russia into an empire at great cost to its people.

veche.name: Veche
veche.summary: A popular assembly among medieval Slavic peoples, especially powerful in Russian cities like Novgorod and Pskov and comparable to the Norse thing; abolished in Pskov in 1510.

iziaslav-i-of-kiev.name: Iziaslav I
iziaslav-i-of-kiev.summary: Prince of Turov and Grand Prince of Kiev at various points between 1054 and 1078; he lived from 1024 to 1078, and his sons Yaropolk and Sviatopolk later ruled Turov.

sviatoslav-ii-of-kiev.name: Sviatoslav II
sviatoslav-ii-of-kiev.summary: Grand Prince of Kiev from 1073 until his death in 1076, a younger son of Yaroslav the Wise who ruled alongside his brothers before seizing the throne from Iziaslav.

rurikids.name: Rurikid dynasty
rurikids.summary: The dynasty founded by Rurik in 862, which ruled Kievan Rus' and its principalities and later the Tsardom of Russia for over 700 years until 1598.

battle-of-kulikovo.name: Battle of Kulikovo
battle-of-kulikovo.summary: 1380 battle in which Dmitry of Moscow defeated the Mongol warlord Mamai, traditionally seen as the turning point when Mongol dominance over Russia began to fade.

tokhtamysh.name: Tokhtamysh
tokhtamysh.summary: Khan of the Golden Horde from 1380 to 1395 (c. 1342-1406) who briefly reunited its two wings, sacked Moscow in 1382, but was later crushed twice by his former ally Timur.

prikaz.name: Prikaz
prikaz.summary: An administrative, judicial or executive office serving palace, civil, military or church authorities in the Grand Duchy of Moscow and Tsardom of Russia, 15th to 18th centuries.

sudebnik-of-1497.name: Sudebnik
sudebnik-of-1497.summary: A collection of laws introduced by Ivan III of Russia in 1497 that helped centralize the Russian state, later replaced by the Sudebnik of 1550.

sophia-palaiologina.name: Sophia Paleologue
sophia-palaiologina.summary: A Byzantine princess of the Palaiologos dynasty who became grand princess of Moscow as the second wife of Ivan III, and grandmother of the first tsar, Ivan IV.

roman-the-great.name: Roman the Great
roman-the-great.summary: Prince of Novgorod, Volhynia and Galicia (1152–1205) who united Galicia and Volhynia, dominated the western regions of Kievan Rus', and died at the Battle of Zawichost in 1205.

volhynia.name: Volhynia
volhynia.summary: A historic region in Central and Eastern Europe spanning parts of Poland, Belarus, and Ukraine, long part of the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth before Russian annexation.

battle-of-zawichost.name: Battle of Zawichost
battle-of-zawichost.summary: A battle fought on 19 June 1205 in which Polish forces under Leszek the White defeated and killed Duke Roman the Great of Galicia-Volhynia, considered one of medieval Poland's greatest victories.

great-stand-on-the-ugra-river.name: Great Stand on the Ugra River
great-stand-on-the-ugra-river.summary: An 1480 standoff on the Ugra River between Akhmat Khan's Great Horde and Grand Prince Ivan III of Moscow, ending with little fighting and often seen as marking the end of Tatar dominance over Russia.
great-stand-on-the-ugra-river.source_title: Great Stand on the Ugra River

andrew-ii-of-hungary.name: Andrew II of Hungary
andrew-ii-of-hungary.summary: Andrew II of Hungary: King of Hungary and Croatia from 1205 to 1235, who also ruled the Principality of Halych on two separate occasions, known for granting royal estates and money to his supporters.

coloman-of-galicia.name: Coloman of Galicia
coloman-of-galicia.summary: Son of Andrew II of Hungary, crowned king of Galicia in 1216 and later duke of Slavonia, captured in battle by Mstislav of Novgorod in 1221.

kingdom-of-galicia-volhynia.name: Galicia–Volhynia
kingdom-of-galicia-volhynia.summary: A medieval state mainly in modern Ukraine, one of the three chief successors of Kievan Rus', whose ruler Daniel was crowned King of Ruthenia in 1253 before Poland absorbed it in 1349.

saint-george.name: Saint George
saint-george.summary: Early Christian martyr who died in 303, said to have been a soldier in the Roman army executed for refusing to renounce his faith; widely venerated and claimed as patron saint by many countries and cities.

vasily-i-of-moscow.name: Vasily I of Moscow
vasily-i-of-moscow.summary: Grand Prince of Vladimir and Moscow from 1389 to 1425, son and heir of Dmitry Donskoy, who allied with and later fought the Grand Duchy of Lithuania.

slavic-paganism.name: East Slavic paganism
slavic-paganism.summary: A polytheistic, nature-focused pre-Christian religion of the Slavic peoples, practiced before their gradual Christianization between the 8th and 13th centuries.

berke.name: Berke Khan
berke.summary: Ruler of the Golden Horde from 1257 to 1266 who established Islam in a Mongol khanate for the first time and allied with the Mamluks against his cousin Hulagu Khan.

zbeg-khan.name: Özbeg Khan
zbeg-khan.summary: Khan of the Golden Horde from 1313 to 1341, its longest-reigning ruler and the leader under whom the state reached its peak.

staryi-krym.name: Staryi Krym
staryi-krym.summary: A small historical city and former bishopric in eastern Crimea, whose name means 'Old Crimea' in several local languages.

hanafi-school.name: Hanafi school
hanafi-school.summary: The largest school of Sunni Islamic law, founded on the teachings of jurist Abu Hanifa (c. 699–767), followed by an estimated 800 million Muslims today.

timur.name: Timur (Tamerlane)
timur.summary: Turco-Mongol conqueror (1320s–1405) who founded the Timurid Empire across Central Asia and the Middle East, seen as one of history's greatest and most brutal military leaders.

giray-dynasty.name: Giray dynasty
giray-dynasty.summary: A Genghisid Turkic dynasty that ruled the Khanate of Crimea from 1431 to 1783, also supplying khans of Kazan and Astrakhan in the 16th century.

pechenegs.name: Pechenegs
pechenegs.summary: A semi-nomadic Turkic people from Central Asia who controlled the steppes of southeast Europe and Crimea in the 9th and 10th centuries, waging over two centuries of wars against Rus'.

russkaya-pravda.name: Russkaya Pravda
russkaya-pravda.summary: The legal code of Kievan Rus', written from the early 12th century onward and based on an earlier 11th-century code, notably lacking capital or corporal punishment.

cossacks.name: Cossacks
cossacks.summary: An East Slavic, Eastern Orthodox militant people from the Pontic-Caspian steppe who defended borders of Poland-Lithuania and Russia in exchange for self-governing autonomy.

don-cossacks.name: Don Cossacks
don-cossacks.summary: Cossacks settled along the Don River who formed an autonomous polity in southern Russia from the late 16th century until 1918, playing a major military role in the Russian Empire.
